cards.title: Six pieces, six personalities
cards.body: King: one square any direction — lose him and the game ends. Queen: any distance, any direction — the strongest piece. Rook: straight lines. Bishop: diagonals. Knight: the L-jump. Pawn: forward one (two on its first move), captures diagonally.

cards.title: The knight is the weirdo — learn it first
cards.body: Every other piece slides. The knight jumps in an L: two squares one way, one square sideways. It leaps over pieces, which makes it the only piece that can open a game with a jump. New players lose to knights more than any other piece.

Starting back rank: rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, bishop, knight, rook.
Memory trick: 'queen loves her color' — the white queen starts on a light square, black queen on a dark one. King goes on the remaining center square.
Play your first ten games focusing on one rule: never leave a piece where the opponent can take it for free. That single habit beats most beginners.

cards.q: Which piece can jump over others?
cards.explain: The knight's L-jump ignores everything in between. Every other piece is blocked by the first thing in its path.

flashcards.back: Your king is under attack — you must get out of it on this move.
Check with no escape. The game ends immediately.
Moves any distance horizontally, vertically, or diagonally — the most powerful piece.
A special pawn capture: if an enemy pawn jumps two squares past yours, you may capture it as if it moved one. It only works on the very next move.

questions.explain: Bishops own the diagonals and never leave their starting color. The L-jump belongs to the knight.
Pawns march straight but eat diagonally — the cause of half of all beginner blunders.

questions.q: What must you do when in check?
choices: Get your king out of attack this move
questions.explain: Check forces a response: move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacker. Ignoring it isn't legal.

questions.q: Where does the white queen start?
questions.explain: 'Queen loves her color': white queen on light, black queen on dark. It's the fastest way to set up correctly.

questions.q: Which piece is worth the most (after the king, who's priceless)?
questions.explain: Standard values: queen 9, rook 5, bishop/knight 3, pawn 1. The queen's range makes her the heavyweight.

cards.title: A fork hits two birds at once
cards.body: A fork attacks two enemy pieces at the same time. The knight is the fork artist — from one square it can stab a king and a rook at once, and your opponent can only save one. Look for enemy pieces sitting a knight's jump apart.

cards.title: A pin freezes a piece in place
cards.body: When a piece can't move without exposing something more valuable behind it, it's pinned. A bishop pinning a knight to the queen is the classic: the knight is stuck, and you can pile attackers onto it for free.

The skewer is a pin in reverse: you attack the valuable piece first, and it must run — abandoning the weaker piece behind it. Rooks and bishops skewer down open lines. Remember: pin the weak to freeze it, skewer the strong to rob it.
Before every move, scan for loose pieces — yours and theirs. A piece with no defenders is a fork or pin waiting to happen. Tactics flow from looseness.

cards.q: Your knight attacks the enemy king and rook at once. That's a…
cards.explain: One piece, two targets, opponent saves only one — the textbook fork. The knight is its natural home.

flashcards.back: One piece attacks two enemy pieces simultaneously.
A piece can't move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it.
Attack the valuable piece so it must move, abandoning the weaker piece behind it.
Moving one piece unveils an attack from another piece hiding behind it.

questions.q: A bishop attacks a knight, and the queen stands behind the knight. The knight is…
questions.explain: The knight can't move without losing the queen — it's pinned to the more valuable piece.

questions.q: Why is the knight the best forking piece?
choices: Its jump hits squares other pieces can't reach together
questions.explain: The knight's L-jump attacks up to eight squares in a pattern nothing else matches, landing forks from nowhere.

questions.q: In a skewer, which piece do you attack first?
choices: The more valuable one, so it must flee
questions.explain: Attack the king or queen; it has to run, and the piece cowering behind it gets left behind.

questions.q: What makes a discovered attack scary?
choices: The unveiled attacker was hidden until the last moment
questions.explain: Your opponent was watching the moving piece, not the bishop lurking behind it. Surprise is the weapon.

questions.q: Your opponent's rook sits undefended. Best mindset?
choices: It's loose — look for a tactic against it
questions.explain: Loose pieces are tactical targets. Scan for forks, pins, and skewers against anything undefended.

cards.title: Openings have three jobs
cards.body: Control the center, develop your pieces, get your king safe. Every good first ten moves does all three. The center (e4, d4, e5, d5) is the high ground — pieces posted there reach everywhere.

cards.title: Develop with threats
cards.body: Don't shuffle the same piece twice while others sleep. Bring knights and bishops out toward the center, castle early (king safety + rook connection in one move), and only then start your plan. Moves that develop and attack at once are golden.

The Italian Game: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4. White stakes the center, develops two pieces, and eyes f7 — the weakest square near Black's king. Simple, principled, and played at every level for 400 years.
Learn ideas, not move lists. 'Control the center, develop, castle' will outscore memorizing twenty moves of theory you don't understand.

choices: King safety plus connecting the rooks
cards.explain: Castling tucks the king behind pawns and brings a rook toward the center — two opening jobs in a single move.

flashcards.back: Own e4/d4/e5/d5 — pieces there reach the whole board.
Moving pieces from their starting squares into active play.
King slides two squares toward a rook; the rook hops over. Only if neither moved and the path is clear.
The 4-move trap (Qh5/Qxf7#). It only works if Black ignores development — principled play refutes it.

questions.q: What's the most important opening goal?
questions.explain: Central control gives your pieces maximum reach. Everything else in the opening serves that.

questions.q: Which square does the Italian Game's bishop eye?
choices: f7 — the weakest square near Black's king
questions.explain: f7 is defended only by the king at the start, making it the classic early target.

questions.q: You moved the same knight three times while your bishops sleep. Problem?
questions.explain: One developed piece three times is worse than three pieces developed once. Bring the army out.

choices: Develop normally — Nc6 blocks it cold
questions.explain: Scholar's mate punishes greed and neglect. Simple developing moves like …Nc6 refute it effortlessly.

questions.q: After 1. e4 e5, a principled second move is…
questions.explain: Nf3 develops a piece toward the center with a threat on e5. Qh5 is premature; a4 develops nothing.
